summary: Verde Vista's own design system, taken from verdevista.net and written down so films, pages and tools can share one look: ink and bone, Lato Light, spaced capitals and hairlines.
context: verdevista.net had a clear look but no system behind it: the values lived in one stylesheet and the decisions in nobody's notes. A film or a tool that wanted to match the site had to guess. Vista writes the site down as tokens, and where the site is silent (a film needs accents, chapter fields and motion the site never uses) it derives the value from the site and records how.
actions: Took every core value from the published site: its stylesheet, its four pages and its splash image.
Made one file the source of truth. tokens.json generates the CSS and the video kit's tokens, so the site, the films and the tools cannot drift apart.
Set a floor for text at 60% bone. The site sets some labels at 50%, which measures 4.42:1 on ink, just under AA, so Vista keeps 50% out of the system.
Derived two accents, a cool haze and a warm ember, from the smoke in the splash image, so they belong to the same light as everything else.
Shipped Lato Light and Regular in the repo under the SIL Open Font License, declared under a name of its own so a renderer uses the files beside the page instead of downloading a copy.

outcomes.claim: Every text pair is contrast checked on every build, and the check fails the build when anything drops under AA or falls out of step with tokens.json.
The Many Heads films on this site, the sizzle on the landing page and the full film, are built on it.

role: Brand films and demo videos, made as code
summary: A Claude Code plugin that makes brand films and app demo videos in the Vista design system, built as code and rendered entirely on your own machine.
context: A short film usually means a timeline editor, stock assets and a look that drifts from everything else the studio makes. Building films as HTML on the design system's own tokens makes every frame reproducible, keeps the look in step with the site, and lets each film pass measured checks before anyone watches it.
actions: Rebuilt an existing video toolkit around Vista: a new design system, the film kit's look, the templates and the documentation.
Brand films: a storyline traced line by line to its sources, a look check before the build, then the film built on a shared kit and rendered locally with HyperFrames, with a composed score.

Demo videos: records a real walkthrough of a web app with Playwright, logs every click, and cuts a titled teaser whose zooms follow the work, in a choice of five tones, with a voiceover or a music version.
Keeps everything local: telemetry off, no cloud rendering, and fonts shipped with each film so nothing is fetched at render time.
Checks every film before it ships: contrast, fonts, audio levels, and motion with no jumps or flashes.

outcomes.claim: Made Vista: Many Heads, a 93 second brand film of my essay “Software isn’t losing its head. It’s growing thousands.”, with a composed piano score, rendered end to end on one machine.
Two skills in one plugin: make-brand-film and make-demo-video.

summary: A single-file browser game that puts you on the FOMC for a year: set the policy rate, watch inflation, unemployment and the Sahm Rule respond.
context: Monetary policy is taught as a set of rules and explained as a set of tradeoffs, but neither conveys what it feels like to make the call with incomplete data and a lag before anything responds. A simulator does.
actions: Built the whole thing as one self-contained HTML file: no build step, no dependencies, and no external requests, so it runs from a file:// URL forever.
Modeled headline PCE, U3 unemployment, the Sahm Rule and the policy rate midpoint, with a news and events feed driving shocks.
Drew the charts on canvas and kept a history panel so a player can see how their own path compares with where they started.

outcomes.claim: Playable right now, in the browser, with no install and no network access.
Makes four indicators legible at once (headline PCE, U3, the Sahm Rule and the policy rate) against decisions the player actually made.

summary: A custom-built AI assistant that helps Davidson students assemble conflict-free four-course schedules for a semester.
context: Course registration at Davidson means satisfying major and minor requirements, the Ways of Knowing distribution, prerequisite chains and registration restrictions, then fitting four courses into a week without collisions. The information needed to do that is spread across a catalog PDF, the WebTree selection flowchart, and whatever a student can find out about instructors. Built as a class project.
actions: Grounded the assistant in four sources: the official Fall 2025 course catalog, the WebTree 2.0 selection logic, RateMyProfessor instructor ratings, and the student's own answers gathered conversationally.
Encoded the rules that make a schedule invalid (prerequisite chains, registration restrictions, time conflicts and credit overloads) so the assistant checks rather than suggests.
Wrote and shipped the tool's limitations alongside it rather than in a footnote.

outcomes.claim: Shipped an assistant that builds conflict-free four-course schedules against Davidson's curriculum requirements, Ways of Knowing distributions and a student's own preferences.
Integrated four separate sources into one conversational interface: course catalog, WebTree selection logic, instructor ratings, and live student input.

Published the tool's own limits with it: that a language model can hallucinate, that it advises rather than registers, and that RateMyProfessor ratings come from small self-selecting samples and should be one factor among many.

role: Custom GPT for a Davidson eating house
summary: An AI assistant for Rusk Eating House that answers on the bylaws, the handbook, the weekly menu and the cleanup rota, with a touch of southern charm.
context: Rusk is a Davidson eating house, established 1977. Everything it runs on lives in four separate documents: a bylaws file, a handbook, a weekly menu and a cleanup schedule. Answering an ordinary question (whose week is it, what is the rule on this, what is for dinner) means knowing which of the four to open, so mostly nobody bothered and the same questions got asked out loud instead.
actions: Grounded the assistant in the house's own documents: the bylaws, the handbook, the weekly menu and the cleanup schedule.
Gave it a voice that fits the house rather than a neutral corporate one, so people would actually use it.
Added event poster generation, so a house event could go from idea to something postable without a designer.
Pointed it at the cleanup rota, so accountability came from a shared source rather than from whoever felt like nagging.

outcomes.claim: Collapsed four scattered house documents into one place anyone can ask, instead of four files nobody opens.
Turned the cleanup schedule into something enforceable, by making whose turn it is a question with an answer.
Generates posters for house events through image generation, so publicity did not depend on finding someone who could design.
